paras: The attempted lynching of the Boyces near Sturgeon was a mob's attempt in May 1881 to lynch two young men named Boyce who had been arrested on the accusation of shooting a farmer's young son ten miles south of Sturgeon. The attempt failed, but the only report found predicted that a lynching would follow if the wounded boy died.

According to a special dispatch from Sturgeon, the two Boyces had caused Enoch Gallop and his wife to separate through what the dispatch called "improper conduct with the woman." Gallop then sold his horses to a Mr. Booth before leaving the country, and the Boyces demanded the horses back.

When Booth refused, the Boyces were said to have gone to his house and hidden near the barn. As Booth and his little boy went to the stable, the two men were accused of firing on them and mortally wounding the boy. News of the shooting reached Sturgeon on Saturday, May 21, the day after it occurred.

The Boyces were arrested, and a mob tried to lynch them during the night before the dispatch was sent. The report gives no place, size or leaders for the mob and does not say how the attempt was stopped.
The dispatch described "great excitement" in the neighborhood and said a lynching would follow if the boy died. No report of the boy's death, a second attempt, or a trial of the Boyces was found.

The Weekly Graphic of Kirksville, Missouri, carried the dispatch on May 27, 1881, as a short paragraph among its editorial notes, between items on Kansas crops and New York senatorial politics. It called the shooting a "dastardly deed" and reported both the mob's attempt and the expected lynching without comment. The item names no race for the Boyces, the mob, or the Booth family.
